## Stadium of Tavyanos

The Stadium of Tavynos was a stadium in the underwater city of Myth Nantar.

Location
This stadium stood along Chamal Avenue, in Myth Nantar's Trade Quarter. It was one of the few structures in the quarter that was untouched by the overgrowth of the Three Gates Reef by 1371 DR.

Structure
This stadium stood three stories tall and had a sublevel, containing a number of cells and staging areas.

History
During the Twelfth Serôs War, the forces of Iakhovas forced the merfolk of Eadraal to abandon their city of Voalidru and a number of other towns, fleeing to the safety of Myth Nantar. The city settled the refugees into the lower levels of the Stadium of Tayvanos, allowing them to turn its cells and staging areas into makeshift homes and hospitals. This arrangement continued for the two years that followed, as the merfolk found it insurmountable to rid Voalidru of the undead left behind by Iakhovas. The mage Jhanra Merlistar was regularly seen among the Stadium's refugees, tending to the injured and teaching their children.

In 1371 DR, a High Merpriest of Eadro named Narvolas joined the refugees, using his expertise to tend to the injured. A few weeks after his arrival to the city, Narvolas was approached by Prince-Regent Mirol III of Eadraal, having been told by a mysterious fish that the priest knew of a way to reclaim Voalidru. Narvolas then informed Mirol III about his experiences during the siege on Voalidru and of an undead repelling relic known as the Akriloth before sending him away.

## Starmara Dagohnlar

Starmara Dagohnlar was a wealthy merchant's wife in the late 14 century DR.

Relationships
Starmara was no longer attracted to her husband, the merchant Durexter Dagohnlar, and at times considered his death. She had a broad network of contacts, good enough that she already knew on sight that Malakar Surth and Aumun Tholant Bezrar, two importers and underworld figures, were working with Harnrim Starangh. She didn't trust her servants one bit.

History
Starmara took Westgate as a place of safety, and had visited it at least once, a house-of-baths being familiar to her.

One night in the early spring of the, Starmara and her husband were taken captive by Malakar Surth and Aumun Tholant Bezrar. She was bound up, and fainted during one of their threats; later, she screamed, conscious again, as her captors were interrupted by Narnra Shalace, a thief from Waterdeep, breaking through the window of the bedroom where all four were present during her escape from Glarasteer Rhauligan, who was in hot pursuit. Her captors attacked the latter, suspecting both crashers of being hired killers; Rhauligan ultimately defeated them both.

Despite Starmara's pleadings, however, they were not rescued, and finally resorted to gnawing away at their bindings. Bezrar escaped shortly after; by dawn, the two Dagohnlars were still cowering, almost certainly still bound, but Malakar also chose to flee rather than slay them.

They were later found by the Guard; while giving a statement, she was rather displeased with her husband's caginess.

## Stag Steads

Stag Steads was a hunting lodge in Cormyr.

Location
The lodge was located near Mouth o' Gargoyles, not far from the road.

Structure
The lodge was built into a hillside, with trees planted ahead of it to better conceal the location and patches of moss over the wood, so it blended into the forest quite well.

Interior
A circular central room contained a hearth big enough to roast three boar or deer at once.

Atmosphere
The place was cool, dim, and damp, other than the central room.

Activities
The lodge was used by the Obarskyr royal family, as well as the three royal noble clans of the Crownsilvers, Huntsilvers, and Truesilvers, and others by invitation only. Being invited to hunt there was something of a coming-of-age tradition among young noblemen. In addition, Vangerdahast had begun holding conferences for War Wizards there during the mid-to-late 1300s DR, and in the 1360s DR, Princess Alusair Obarskyr and some of the younger Huntsilvers would take lovers there for a few days, so many non-noble guests had come to spend some nights there and enjoyed the privilege of staying and hunting at Stag Steads.

Most visitors spent no more than six or seven days in the lodge, and a few up to a tenday. Anyone who tried staying beyond this limit would be asked to leave, politely at first, and then by Royal Magician in person.

Despite the frequency of hunting, the hunting was still good, partially because of a local deepspawn placed there by the orders of the Royal Mage.

Services
People staying there were able to go up to a side window and order a plate of food for 1 gp, wine for 4 gp, and a flagon of regular ale for 2 gp in the 1360s DR. The platters had a unique design, and were the customer's to keep.

Those meals consisted of fern-and-fiddlehead soup, morels, and other vegetables from the forest, served with meat from roast boar, venison, or grouse. The menu seldom varied during the late 14 century DR, but the cook was excellent and found ways to add variety, while the wine cellar was top-notch in Volo's appreciation. Meals were free to guests.

Most guests left the steads with barrels of salted meat, whether hunted themselves or by the guides, and sometimes with a mounted head. Locals were available to stuff and mount heads for 5–10 gp each.

Guests were free to wander the area as they willed, but non-regulars were recommended to hire a guide. There were official guides, marked by their badges, who were available to aid anyone in hunting and forestry. Their fares were 1 to 6 gp daily, depending on who and for what. For an extra gold piece or two, they would also guide their charge to some nearby ruins.

Defenses
A gate inside a rear room connected the place with the Palace of the Purple Dragon in Suzail, and was often used to pass stones with messages wrapped around them through, but also royals, War Wizards, and retainers.

When senior War Wizards were in attendance, they were quick in resorting to magically enhanced interrogation to determine both powers and intentions of travelers arriving without invitation. Other War Wizards scried on anyone who lingered.

History
Originally it had been a druid's home, then an ogre's keep, and then a hunting lodge. The lodge was forfeited to the Crown after the treason of the last Goldfeather noble, who was executed by King Dhalmass Obarskyr in the .

In the, before teleporting Caladnei and Myrmeen Lhal to Vangerdahast Aeiulvana's sanctum, Elminster Aumar claimed they were headed to Stag Steads.

Staff
The strongest recommendations for hiring a guide came from Bald Jhawn. The best of the badged foresters was generally considered Tlumbel Droun; other names included Ithaglor Bruensal, Dreth Milyntyr, and Doalogh Dultor. A local, working two cottages away from the Steads, and the best at mounting heads, was known as Old Martha.

Rumors & Legends
There were often hunts for a "Ghost Stag", a giant white stag said to vanish when cornered. The War Wizards insisted the Ghost Stag was psionic, rather than undead.

## Staff of Silverymoon

A staff of Silverymoon was a unicorn-headed magical staff given to the High Mages of Silverymoon once they began their rule. Each staff had a variety of magical abilities, fitting their status as an emblem of the Gem of the North, many of which were tied to the city's own wards and enchantments.

Description
The body of a staff of Silverymoon was made from a thin, dark wood, and carried atop it a carving of a unicorn's head.

Powers
In Silverymoon
Due to their special importance to the Gem of the North, the staffs of Silverymoon could also affect the city's most notable feature, the Moonbridge. Not only was such a staff capable of activating or ending the Moonbridge itself, but it could also make the bridge radiate moonfire, turning it visible, as well as reversing gravity across either segments or the whole of the Moonbridge for a few seconds.

Within the High Palace
Being a symbol of rulership, the staffs of Silverymoon also held a unique ability tied directly to the Silver Throne from which the High Mage governed. If they held their staff while sitting atop the throne, the magic infused into both would render the High Mage entirely immune to all magic, with the only two exceptions being a wish spell or that of the Lady of Mysteries herself, Mystra.

As the High Palace of Silverymoon contained many layered wards, the staffs further acted as a token for any and all of them, giving the High Mage a unique freedom within the palace walls. Where others were barred from entering or from casting certain spells, the possession of a staff of Silverymoon outranked even the power of these ancient dweomers. Furthermore, each staff was magically linked to other major ward tokens. With only a minor amount of concentration, anyone wielding a staff of Silverymoon was not only capable of locating these tokens within a radius of, but also of identifying whoever was using it. The staff could expand the liberties of those tokens, often amulets or rings of mithral, as well as restrict them, taking away their privileged exemptions to the wards. This last ability, however, was known only to the High Mages.

Just as a staff of Silverymoon allowed its wielder to step through the palace's various wards unmolested, it also served as a kind of key, the only thing capable of opening the hidden doors leading into the palace's lowest four dungeon levels. One such door led to the High Mage's Crypt, holding no lock for it had no actual key, while another, more secretive entryway connected the depths of Lady Hope's Tower to a treasure room beneath the High Mage's Keep.

Though the rulers of Silverymoon coyly avoided confirming any rumors, some people even believed that a staff of Silverymoon was capable of awakening the stone unicorns that decorated the walls of the High Palace with only a touch.

In General
The wielder of a staff of Silverymoon could, with only a moment's concentration, flawlessly intuit the exact place where any other staff was to be found. This ability had no limit, being confined only by the borders of Realmspace.

A staff of Silverymoon allowed the High Mage to teleport to any of the other staffs or, conversely, teleport them to the High Mage. This was an intrinsic element of the staff, and so carried no chance for error, nor was there any barrier (none, at least, known to the High Mages) capable of blocking a staff of Silverymoon from teleporting when called. In the instance that a High Mage attempted to teleport to a staff that was entirely confined by a solid, however, they would be made aware of it before being transported. This, then, allowed them to choose whether they wanted to instead teleport to a safe position nearby the staff or to not teleport at all.

The staff's ability to create the Moonbridge was partially channeled through certain magical totems that were inlaid beneath the shores of the River Rauvin, but this was only because of the Moonbridge's sheer size. In any other situation, a staff of Silverymoon can still create similar bridges, measuring  in width and  in length. Any larger a gap and the construct simply hovered, extended to its limit but firmly rooted, one end to the ground and the other to the middle of the air. Whether or not it reached the other side, any bridge created by a staff of Silverymoon provided steady ground on which anyone could walk.

A staff of Silverymoon also automatically conferred protections akin to a greater spell immunity spell onto any and all who were touching it. The wielder of the staff could further induce a restoration effect, though this was not automatic, and could only be done once every tenday.

Each staff allowed its wielder to cast a selection of spells every day, though the number of times each could be used varied. Of the highest frequency was hold monster, which a staff of Silverymoon could cast six times in the span of one day. Thrice a day, such a staff could grant its wielder the ability to know alignment or fly, and was also capable of forming a wall of force, while twice a day, it had the power to animate rock or create a passwall. Only once every day was a staff of Silverymoon able to form a minor globe of invulnerability, a forcecage, chain lightning, or a dimension door. This last one was the most unique, as it was another effect that could be extended to anyone touching the staff at the same time, each one being transported wherever they willed, no matter if they all shared their target destination or not.

History
The history of the staffs of Silverymoon was almost as long as that of the High Mages themselves. Their legacy began in the  with the second of these ruling wizards, Aglanthol the Red, who made and enchanted his duskwood staff himself. From then on, each High Mage had their own, unique staff of Silverymoon made, and carried it throughout their time in office.

The second of these staffs was held by the third High Mage, Ederan Nharimlur. However, forty-seven years into his rule, in the, his staff of Silverymoon was stolen by members of the Brotherhood of the Black Hand and never recovered. As of 1370 DR, the staff still remained in the crumbling ruins of Hellgate Keep.

The staff of the ninth High Mage, Orjalun, was left with his apprentice, Sepur, who would himself become the tenth ruler of Silverymoon. After Sepur left the Gem of the North only two years into his High Mageship, his staff of Silverymoon served as one of his few identifying remains in the Evermoors, where it lay shattered and surrounded by scorch marks.

Once their respective High Mage was interred in the palace's crypt, most staffs were moved there as well, held in the grasp of a marble statue of their past owner. Even Orjalun's staff of Silverymoon rested above his empty bier.

As of the mid-to-late 14 century, beyond the ones owned by Alustriel Silverhand and Taern Hornblade, the two High Mages at the time, there were also at least two more staffs of Silverymoon across the North. Both were hidden, one in the Harper base of Moongleam Tower, in nearby Everlund, and the other in Waterdeep's Blackstaff Tower. It was rumored, though unconfirmed, that even more could be found beyond the Savage North. Some suggested that they were located in various catacombs, but the more common claims said there was one at the Herald's Holdfast and another was kept by Lady Saharel of Spellgard.

Notable Staffs of Silverymoon
 Rather than carrying atop it the Silvaeren symbol of the unicorn's head, Ederan Nharimlur's stolen duskwood staff was crowned with the head of a cat.  It could cast spell turning and globe of invulnerability twice, as well as darkvision, alter self, and cat's grace once, before needing to recharge.

## Stumble Guys

Stumble Guys is a battle royale party game created by Kitka Games in 2021 and later acquired, developed and published by American developer Scopely. In 2023, it had an official collaboration with Dungeons & Dragons, with Forgotten Realms–related content and characters appearing in a 2-week-long limited-time game mode from March 28 to April 11.

Description

Copying the format of Fall Guys, the game has players run through different obstacle courses and survive other situations until only one winning player remains. It includes various other game modes as well. Players may purchase or win costumes and emotes for their avatars.

In the "Stumbles & Dragons" D&D game mode, there are three rounds. First, players must run through a dungeon decorated with symbols of the Cult of the Dragon, with eyes modified to those of the typical blank-eyed Stumble Guys character. They must negotiate obstacles like dart traps, swinging blades and spikes, moving platforms, kobolds, gelatinous cubes, a beholder's eye rays, and a red dragon launching a moving fiery beam, lest they fall into lava and respawn. A moving "prismatic wall" in the rear eliminates players who fall behind. This continues until a set number remain. Second, the players are in "Lava Land", where they must jump to different hexagons to escape rising lava. In the third and final level, players go through the dungeon again until only one remains as the winner. In the dungeon rounds, players are assigned a "class" with unique powers: the fighter can swing a magical axe to clear an obstacle and boost speed; a wizard may teleport to another point in the map; a rogue may jump further; and a cleric may use a holy shield to gain invulnerability to hazards. All players receive the same class, which is selected at random each round. No story or characterization is attached to this game.

During the event, players could purchase from the in-game shop or earn through the current battle pass battle pass various D&D-themed costumes and emotes. Costumes include "The Sage" (an unnamed Elminster), Wizard of Thay, Drow Rogue, Human Bard, Dragonborn Paladin, Githyanki Fighter, Tiefling Warlock, Owlbear, Animated Armor, and more.

This collaboration is a result of D&D-owner Hasbro's dealings with the Public Investment Fund (PIF) of Saudi Arabia; the PIF wholly owns Savvy Games Group, which in turn owns Scopely. This has resulted in several other collaborations and licensing deals, including other licensed characters and game modes in Stumble Guys (such as Nerf) and other games. This was criticized by Rascal News as being part of an effort to "sportswash" or distract from negative aspects of Saudi Arabia's reputation.

The Staff of Cherished Necromancy was a unique mage's staff that once belonged to Cherish Hollow, the necromancer author of The Amiable Art of Necromancy sometime before the late 15 century DR.

The staff's head was always lit with sinister green flames and the entire shaft radiated a necrotic magical glow. It possessed a +2 enchantment that made the weapon's swings more deadly and guided it toward the targets. Additionally, each strike landed with the Staff of Cherished Necromancy dealt additional necrotic damage. The wielder also had their necromancy magic heightened, greatly increasing their chances of the necromantic spells affecting the targets. All creatures that were slain with the wielder's necromancy spells had their life essence harvested and stored within the staff, allowing the wielder to cast additional necromancy spells from any circle of magic without erasing them from the caster's memory.

History
Sometime before the, the Staff of Cherished Necromancy belonged to Cherish Hollow. But by some undisclosed means, the staff ended up in the hands of a powerful mummy lord of Baldur's Gate known as the Mystic Carrion. The staff and its undead master could be found in Philgrave's Mansion in the Gate's Lower City.

In the aftermath of the Council of the Dragon and ensuing massacre on late Mirtul of the, Broryn Windstag, who had remained at home for the event, had Irlin Stonestable as a guest when his servant Aereld informed him of the chaos in the wake of the killing. Though he felt it may have been exaggerated, a soon-arriving Sacrast Handragon confirmed Aereld and explained the situation was even more dire.

## Still Waters (Shadowfell)

Still Waters was the name of a haunted swamp in the Shadowfell.

Description
The waters were cold and dark, and appeared to be entirely motionless. If any living creature saw its own reflection in these waters, the reflection animated as a spirit of shadow and attempted to strangle the creature that cast it.

The swamp was inhabited. Rickety paths of cut trees connected huts that sat atop stilts.

Geography
Still Waters lay along the Shadowfell Road somewhere between Endless Alleys and Veil. The road was made of lashed-together logs, and vehicles had to be careful when traversing this stretch. Other paths branched out in different directions, potentially making the road difficult to follow.

The swamp was home to various shadowborn who wore blindfolds so as not to see their own reflections in the waters. ## Stomacher

A stomacher was a type of underbodice in Faerûn, similar to a corset, that was worn by women overtop of gowns or other silken dress.

Stomachers were rigid garments that extended from crotch the wearer's crotch to their breast. Many offered support for a wearer's breasts as well as shaped panels for the hips. And stomachers that were made to cinch tight a wearer's waist tight were particularly popular.

Waterdhavian stomachers often swept the sides of the bodice into fanciful swirls and gave off pointed shoulders.

In the mid-to-late 14 century DR, stomachers were a common element of fashion among younger Waterdhavian noble ladies. The stomachers worn by such women were of an open wire-work type, sporting elaborate filigree and designs, often set with gemstones.

In the, silver-laced stomachers were all the rage among Selgauntan noblewomen. Many wore them to the annual ball that was held on Hammer 30 in Stormweather Towers by Thamalon Uskevren to commemorate his lost brother. Notable wearers at the ball included members of House Uskevren, such as Shamur Uskevren wore a gold stomacher and her daughter Thazienne Uskevren who wore a bejeweled silver stomacher.

## Stuffed toy

Stuffed toys, also known as fabric dolls and typically referred to in everyday speech as softfurries, were a type of toy doll with an outer fabric sewn from a textile and stuffed with flexible material. Though typically made for children, there were also comfort cuddlers for adults and they were sometimes enjoyed by pets as chewtoys.

Description
They toys were distinguishable from other dolls mainly by their softness, being made of textile materials such as felt and stuffed with feathers. or felt.

Stuffed toys varied greatly in appearance. They were commonly made to resemble animals, though one could also find dolls made to resemble humans, demihumans, or monsters, such as owlbears. Cats were among the most popular of animal depictions, whilst stuffed bears were uncommon.

Availability

 Aurora's Whole Realms Catalogue sold a line of fabric dolls that were imported from various places across Faerûn, such as Waterdeep and cities around the Dragon Sea, at a price of 3 silver pieces. These dolls were made from the highest-quality cloth and stuffed with both feathers and felt. This range of dolls consisted of male and female commoners, non-denominational priests, rogues, sorcerers, warriors, and princes and princesses. The adventurer dolls (those depicting priests, rogues, sorcerers, and warriors) came with soft stuffed weaponry. Special orders could be made to tailor cleric dolls to particular faiths or alignments. And by default these dolls were made to resemble humans, though special orders could be made for ones resembling dwarves, elves, gnomes, or halflings.
 Collar The Beast, the oldest attraction at the Jack Mooney & Sons Circus, offered stuffed animals that could be exchanged for prize tokens. For three tokens they offered small ones, worth a single silver piece, while five tokens could be exchanged for a large one worth around two to five silver pieces.
 Magnificent Mergatroid's Traveling Troupadors had a variety of small to large stuffed toys that could be won from its carnival games.
 The Toysmiths, a toyshop in Ravens Bluff that was owned and operated by the gnome brothers Gunder and Relvan Gaewilder, sold a similar range of dolls as Aurora's Catalogue. However, the brothers charged differently for each type of doll. Commoners, non-denominational priests, rogues, and warriors were sold for 3 silver pieces. Princes and princesses were sold for 4 silver pieces. And sorcerers or sorceresses were sold for 5 silver pieces. For an extra charge of 2 sp, they would tailor their priest dolls to specific religions.
 Traagor's Tours and Souvenir Shop in Ravens Bluff sold plush toys resembling King, a dog that was locally famous in the city in the 14 century DR, that were made for them by the Toysmiths.

Notable Stuffed Toys
 Angelica's magical stuffed toy, an enchanted stuffed owlbear that belonged to a small Ravenian girl named Angelica Turgon. It had a Waukeenar pendant sewn into its neck and could summon a real owlbear.
 Arabel's huggable bear, an enchanted stuffed bear that protected sleepers from bad dreams and mind-affecting magic.
 Doll golems, a variety of golem made from a singular child's toy, could be fashioned from a stuffed toy.
 Esmae's magical stuffed toy, an enchanted stuffed animal that Esmae Amarantha gifted to Vid, an oni that was trapped in Barovia. It could transform into a large creature that would fight on Vid's behalf. This creature was variously said to be either a brown bear, giant ape, or giant crocodile. Once slain, the creature would transform into an inanimate, giant-sized stuffed toy.
 Jebediah's magical stuffed toy, an enchanted stuffed bear that belonged to a small boy named Jebediah. It would radiate magic circle against evil as a  sphere whenever its owner was in a natural state of slumber. Sleep that was induced by either magic or poison would not trigger the effect.

Notable Owners
 Angelica Turgon.
 Ash, a young girl that lived in the town of Fullpoint in the late 14 century DR.
 Callie, a small child in Ravens Bluff, owned a stuffed bear doll golem named Cuddle.
 The ghosts of children that haunted the Endless Alleys in the Shadowfell were often seen holding stuffed animals that emitted unnerving giggling that rang throughout the corridors.
 Jebediah, a small boy that got lost in the Domains of Dread. He managed to hide his enchanted stuffed toy before he was murdered by the domain's lord Vall and later gifted it to a group of Ravenian adventurers that later visited the domain.
 The Nesper family of Nightstone had a stuffed bear that was taken by the goblins Blik and Flik when their clan ransacked the town.
 Portrait Balls, a portrait business in the Jack Mooney & Sons Circus, kept stuffed animals on hand that could be used as props in portraits.
 Shyla, a young Ravenian orphan turned adventurer, owned a stuffed bear.
 Taleena, a young girl in the Vast that owned a stuffed mammoth.
 Wendy, a small girl in Ravens Bluff, owned a stuffed bear.
 Zox Clammersham kept a stuffed toy for his pet giant badger.

## Steelsky Liberators

The Steelsky Liberators were a group of rebel crusaders and dragon slayers who fought to free the lands of Abeir from draconic oppression since ancient times.

History
The Steelsky Liberators were founded in ancient times on Abeir, when a group of rebel crusaders learned to use the power of an ancient divine blessing on the arambar that was granted to mortals to combat dragons. The group vowed to free those under the yoke of dragons and to watch over and protect the lands that were free of dragons. These rebels operated mainly in the lands of Laerakond.

After the Spellplague of, the practices of the Steelsky Liberators spread into Faerûn when some of the dragonborn and genasi crusaders that survived this catastrophe were transported to the lands of Faerûn. They were among the founders of the kingdoms of Tymanther and Akanûl, and passed on their abilities to individuals that were seeking more power and knowledge to defeat dragons oppressing their lands.

Abilities
The abilities of the Steelsky Liberators were of divine nature, and were focused to kill dragons or creatures of elemental nature. The practices of the Steelsky Liberators also granted a degree of resistance against charm and fear abilities.

## Stonechild

Stonechildren were creatures born to a union of a mortal and an elemental – people of stone and dirt, whose origins were on the Elemental Plane of Earth.

Description
Stonechild men and women were similar in appearance to bulky muscular humanoids, but had rock-like rough gray skin. They did not have hair, and their eyes were gray or black with very rare gem-hues. But even at a cursory glance, a stonechild was very obviously an elemental creature. They rarely wore clothes beyond what was utilitarian and most often were armed with massive two-handed greatswords. Stonechildren possessed a keen mind, impressive fortitude, and incredible strength.

An average stonechild grew to the height of almost  and could weigh more than, with average males being slightly bigger and heavier than average females.

Personality
Most stonechildren loved showing their strength, eagerly accepted challenges, and valued individuality and resilience above all else. They never panicked nor acted irrationally, often hiding their feelings behind a stern facade and practical thinking. Stonechildren did not find social conflicts to be productive, and instead of openly stating their disdain for someone, they simply left the person's company without attracting any attention to themselves. Most prided themselves on their internal feeling of honor, with was in balance with understanding and following of laws and rules, but still possessing a goodly nature and having compassion towards others.

Stonechild found kinship with races of stone, especially dwarves, were friendly with humans, and generally got along with all people. Elves and gnomes often felt uneasy around stonechildren, thinking their strength and size to be too alien, and, in turn, stonechildren found it hard to relate to and understand elves' minds. However, halflings and stonechildren got along great, often traveling together.

Abilities

All stonechildren could cast the magic stone spell. They were fully immune to all poisons and acids and possessed darkvision that reached .

Combat
In battle, a stonechild was unyielding, eagerly taking on challenging foes.

Society
Most commonly, stonechildren were born in human and dwarf communities from which they were rarely ostracized and exiled. After reaching maturity, few stonechildren born on the Prime Material plane remained lone wanderers, often becoming adventurers. Their nature guided stonechildren to find homes underneath mountains, which often allowed them to find home among the dwarves, practicing battles and stonework. However, as they aged, stonechildren began experiencing a longing for the Elemental Plane of Earth, and most eventually found their way to the elemental planes and settled among their own kind. Stonechildren that were born in the planes or those who wound their way there, tended to live their lives on the Elemental Plane of Earth and shared values with other beings of the stone, such as dwarves. Stonechildren were only summoned to other worlds and planes by powerful magics, usually to be used as soldiers under someone's control.

Stonechildren did not have their own religion and ended up following the deities of the communities they were born into or joined after finding a home. Most stonechildren respected Moradin's mastery over stone even if they did not necessarily worship the dwarvish god.

They spoke both Common and Terran, and despite preferring Terran, stonechildren were intelligent enough to learn new languages swiftly. The most common other language among them was Dwarvish. Their naming convention was somewhat similar to that of the dwarves but lacked the Stout Folks' rigid naming rules. Each new generation of stone children created their own last names and naming conventions, and their first names were often derived from the Common Tongue.

History
By the late 14 century DR, stonechildren were found inhabiting Undermountain on the Sword Coast North. The hamlet of Spiderhaven counted fifty stonechildren abound its inhabitants, with Chief Constable Sheru'Tan being among the communities authority figures.

## Starsunder

Starsunder was an elf originally of Myth Drannor.

Personality
He was welcoming, but really wanted his secrets kept.

Description
He wore a blue open-breasted shirt, leather breeches, and high boots. He also had a dark-green half cloak.

Activities
He was privy to matters of phaerimm, malaugrym, and sharn.

Abilities
He was capable of learning about damage to distant forests at will, and knew where a number of portals were. One of his spells or abilities was at the same time defensive and aggressive in use, allowing him to parry away spells and strike down foes with a single casting; the spell-shield could also be turned into a web and hurled at foes.

Possessions
He had two teardrop-shaped objects hovering near his head.

History
At the moment of his birth, a fallen star struck the ground and he was named after the event. When he was young, he was a witness to the argument between Coronal Eltargrim Irithyl and Lady Ildilyntra Starym before she attempted to kill him, though he kept the secret close to his chest.

In the, Starsunder was at Tangletrees, where he met the mage Umbregard of Galadorna. Umbregard was looking for guidance related to Elminster Aumar, who was both the last court mage of his land and a Chosen of Mystra. The grove sacred to Rillifane Rallathil and Sehanine Moonbow judged Umbregard sincere, and Starsunder spoke freely with him. He later took Umbregard to the Lookout Tree, where he explained the tasks before Elminster, and also the risk that Elminster's temptations became suffering for someone else. Afterwards, he took him across the sea to the forest near Starmantle, at the Dead Place, where fires had been used in disregard of the safety of the woods.

In the forest, they met with a number of Sharran Dreadspells, who attacked them. Though Umbregard and Starsunder fought, they only prevailed at great cost, with Umbregard injured, and thanks to the timely intervention of Tenthar Taerhamoos, a foe of his guest. Both Starsunder and Umbregard tried to heal Starsunder afterwards. They stabilized him sufficiently for Elminster Aumar to arrive and heal the elf; afterwards, all four had some wine for a toast.

## Stabilize chaos

Stabilize chaos was an alteration spell developed by planeswalker wizards to give them a reprieve while on the plane of Limbo.

While sentient beings in Limbo normally had to concentrate to maintain a pocket of stable reality, the stabilize chaos spell acted in place of such concentration, maintaining stable reality pockets whilst the casters busied themselves with other matters. This spell could only maintain the stability of a stable reality pocket, not increase its size or initiate the creation of one. Stabilize chaos lasted for a minimum of 1 hour and 10 minutes, but could last longer depending on the prowess of the spellcaster.

Outside of Limbo itself, this spell could also be utilized on any chaos matter that had somehow found its way outside of the plane.

Components
Casting this spell required only somatic and verbal components.

Sometime in the 14 century DR, a duergar sage living in Acheron by the name of Gheldoin gifted a spellbook containing stabilize chaos to a group of Ravenian adventurers after they impressed him by deciphering the script on an old scroll that detailed a story about Laduguer.

Stone biters were a type of arrow with heads specially designed for the purpose of attaching ropes to battlements, walls, or other structures. They required careful craftsmanship to produce.

Description
Stone biters had narrow, heavy heads made of high-quality metal, with small ridges in place of the barbs one would find a wood biter arrow. They were usually sharpened to the greatest extent possible. Standard stone biters could provide a grip for relatively soft stone structures, such as those made of brick or sandstone, but those that used adamantine in their manufacture were capable of biting into all but the hardest of stone surfaces.

Availability
 Some metalsmiths in the city of Ravens Bluff were known to produce stone biter arrows, including ones made with adamantine.

## Steam engine

Steam engines were a variety of heat engines that used steam to power mechanical processes. They were known to be created by artificer rock gnomes, members of the Church of Gond, members of the Church of Thoth, and by the clockwork mages of Zakhara.

Usages
 Some of the clockwork creations of clockwork mages were powered by steam engines, though such creations were few and far between, being rather dangerous to build.
 In the land of Mulhorand the priests of Thoth devised a way to utilize steam engines in conjunction with dams to harness the power of the nation's rivers for the purposes of grinding grain and pumping water out into the farther reaches of Mulhorand's desert.
 The steam dragon, a crude vehicle outfitted with a steam engine that was on display in the Hall of Wonders.
 The Revenge, a Zhentil Keep naval vessel that was secretly worked on by Gondar in 1368 DR, had a steam engine to supplement its sails. However, the engine only worked in brief intervals, allowing the ship much needed maneuverability during naval confrontations.

Reputation
In the latter half of the 14 century DR, the coat of arms for the nation of Lantan featured steam engines. The top half of the coat of arms displayed a working steam engine, represented by a complex knot of continuous pipes and valves overlying a circular boiler, and surrounded by a scalloped circle of orange that represented the steam lit by the flames of the engine’s out-of-view firebox. The bottom half of the coat of arms displayed an exploding steam engine, represented by a cloud of gray steam with a leaning smokestack protruding out from the upper right, as pistons and their linkages flew out from the left left and center left of the cloud, and in its center pinwheel of orange flames.

History
The use of steam technology in the nation of Mulhorand came to an end when one of the pharaohs decreed a ban on all further development, feeling that technological innovation had gone too far once proposals were made to build a huge dam on the River of Spears. Most of the nation's steam engines fell into disrepair, though a few powered by stones of everburning continued to pump water into isolated areas. Around 1357 DR, a small faction within the Church of Thoth known as the Technologists picked up the work on steam technology in secrecy, seeking to rediscover the lost knowledge of their predecessors and discover further uses for the technology.

Around the 14 century DR, a community of gnomes living in the Vast were obsessed with creating or innovating upon the steam engine, which they referred to as the "Grand Design". They kept the Grand Design under the cover of a tent to protect it from rain. They were convinced that if they succeeded in their efforts they could bring about a new age of leisure and enlightenment to Faerûn.

In addition to feverishly and tirelessly working towards the Grand Design, many of the gnomes within the community tinkered with potential devices to be powered by the steam engine. These included such things as back scratchers, tooth brushes, multi-tiered pipe organs, sausage grinders, as well as devices to trim the hairs of a nose, paint a tent, wash a crock, or clean filth from one's ears or toes.

The chief engineer of this project was one Sassafras Thompson, with his assistants Broccoli Higgins and Rhubarb Smith. Despite the best efforts of Sassafras and his assistants, everyone in their little community was convinced that they alone knew what was the best way to improve upon the Grand Design and thus were prone to tinkering with it without permission. Prior to Sassafras the project was headed by one Leapold Manfeld, who was close to perfecting the Grand Design, but left out of frustration over the frequent unpermitted modifications done by the other gnomes. Later, unhampered by the interference of the other gnomes, Leapold managed to construct his own perfectly working steam engine and had it installed on a prototype submarine.

Due to all this tinkering, tests with these experimental engine often lead to explosions down the mountainside. This caused terrible tremors in the surrounding area, leading to the instability and collapse of the mines of the Torn Tartan clan of dwarves. The chieftain of the Torn Tartans, Boris, attempted to reason with the gnomes but to no avail.

## Sternhelm

King Sternhelm, more commonly known by his moniker – The Mad King, was a dwarvish ruler of the great stronghold of Keldegonn in the Dragonbone Vale of the Sword Mountains long before the 15 century DR.

History
Many centuries before the 15 century DR, King Sternhelm was a ruler who wanted to leave a great legacy for his people; however, that was not to be. One day, he noticed a glimmer of something valuable while riding past an ancient ruin. Curious, the king followed the sine and discovered a bejeweled chalice peaking from under some rubble. The chalice did not look like it was forged by a dwarvish hand, so the king took it with him as a precious exotic souvenir. Using the chalice as a drinking cup, Sternhelm began being plagued by ghostly whispers. Unbeknownst to him, the chalice was an ancient Netherese ritual vessel from the ruin that held the dark artifact, the Scaleblight Mythallar. The curse got worse, and the spirits from the Shadowfell slowly drove the monarch to madness. When the Mad King perished, his own spirit was absorbed by the chalice.

Every individual who used the chalice became possessed by the Mad King's spirit. In the late 15 century DR, an unlucky dwarvish adventurer who ventured into the Dragonbone Vale fell victim to Sternhelm's ghost. Posessed, the mad dwarf became a danger to the locals, and a bounty was put on his head. It was presumed that the adventurer was slain, but the chalice's fate remained unknown.

## Storna Harnwood

Darklady Storna Harnwood was a priestess of Shar and leader of the Night Brigade gang in Wheloon Prison in the late 15 century DR. She lead the Night Brigade from the Temple of Shar she had built atop the ruins of the Riverside Rats' former homes.

Description

Storna had pale skin, gray eyes, and long black hair.

Personality

Storna was wholly devoted to Shar and the tenets of the faith. She was cold, dispassionate, and ruthless in her goals. While a powerful and wealthy gang leader, she was unlike the others in that she considered the material boons secondary to the glorification of Shar. According to her cook, she ate the same supper every night—a simple and plain dish of meat and potatoes.

Possessions

Storna wore a suit of glossy black half-plate and carried a round small shield and ornate mace. She accessorized with a special pendant and a circlet of Shar.

Though fabulously wealthy from her time as gang leader, she discarded the treasure she had accumulated and let shadows play with it, and her personal quarters were a solitary space with little beyond an austere collection of shabby old furniture scattered about.

History

Storna led the Night Brigade from strength to strength through ruthlessness and guile. After years of work, their power was solidified inside the prison when they attacked and nearly destroyed the far less militant Riverside Rats gang of wererats, taking their hideout and transforming it into a Temple of Shar. The few survivors escaped through the Wererat's Entrance to the exterior of the prison, where they recruited some opportunistic allies to lead the counterattack. After the slaying of her lieutenants Master Thief Karissa, Battlemaster Agarta, and her Grand Arcanist Darstil Vurusk, Garmor the Grim set a mission to finish off Storna and destroy the gang once and for all. With the subtle assistance of Selûne helping to dispel the darkness and despair that filled the temple, the avengers broke through Storna's devotees and living shadow defenders, finally meeting her in battle. Storna wasn't even upset at her lieutenants being killed and her gang being destroyed, as that was the very essence of the final truth that Shar embodied. She met her end stoically, knowing that she had fulfilled her duty to the goddess as best she could.

## Staenyn

Staenyn was a Sharran priest in the mid-14 century DR.

Abilities
He could cast Spider of Shar.

Relationships
He served under the Temple Master Maeldur.

History
In, Staenyn was at a certain Thayvian temple of Shar where the Red Wizard Azmyrandyr was quartered at the time. The Red Wizard was targetted for elimination by the Simbul in response to an attack on Silverymoon on which he participated. After she slew Azmyrandyr and all his apprentices, she proceeded to slay all nearby Red Wizards and the temple staff; Temple Master Maeldur called on Staenyn to rouse two visitors, one of which he deemed mightier than Azmyrandyr: Ylondan the Tall and Largrond of the Lash.

Staenyn got them to join the fray, but he was then tripped by Ylondan, and slain by a blade barrier the Simbul had hijacked and rendered mobile with her magic, which she sent down his way while he was still down.

He was a Zhentarim.

Strabbin Stillcorn's look was known by Storm Silverhand from her time scrying on Manshoon.

## Steward of the Grove

A Steward of the Grove, also known as a Watcher over the Grove, was a powerful druid of the Earthmother who acted as a caretaker and guardian of a Great Grove on the Moonshae Isles.

Activities
Once a druid became a sufficiently powerful spellcaster, they were eligible to have a Great Grove entrusted to their care. These Stewards' primary duty was to tend to the moonwell at the center of their grove. They spent most of their time cleansing the moonwell as they spoke prayers to the Earthmother. If not tending to this duty, they were never far away and could be swiftly summoned. They took their duties incredibly seriously, and valued the sanctity of their moonwell over their own lives.

Stewards were also entrusted with overseeing other druids. They were always accompanied by two lesser (although still quite powerful) druid guardians, and if unable to tend to their duties for some reason, they enlisted another powerful druid to assist them.

Stug Minedale was hired thug who was hired to break knees by Uktar, the bursar of the Guild in the city of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Description
Stug was a gold dwarf with a brown skin tone, brown eyes, and brown hair with a bushy beard.

History
In the, Stug offered his knee-breaking services to the Guild as a reminder of the coin owed by its many debtors. Despite his unsavory occupation, his family member, Gherva Minedale, offered the thug the opportunity to join the Vigilant Knights order of lawful and goodly warriors on one condition – Stug was to stop beating people up for the Guild. This posed a dilemma that the two discussed over a drink or ten at the Elfsong Tavern in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate. Stug insisted that he had already taken the money from Uktar for beating someone up, and going back on the agreement was akin to oath-breaking. Gherva, however, remained stern, stating that if he were to do that job for the Guild, Stug could kiss the Vigilant Knights membership goodbye. Eventually, Stug agreed to return Uktar's coin but was afraid that his own knees would be broken as a result.

## Storm (light hammer)

Storm was a variety of enchanted light hammer created on the Sword Coast North in the late 14 century DR, with its origins dating to the time Cimbar became the capital of Chessenta.

Powers
There existed three variants of the Storm hammer, each possessed a +1, +2, and +8 enchantments that made the hammerhead's bludgeoning damage deadlier and guided the wielder's hand towards the target. All three versions were ensorcelled to deal lightning damage with each strike. The +2 and +8 variants also offered the wielder resistance to normal and magical electricity.

Storm could be created from an enchanted light hammer and a diamond.

History
The oldest and strongest variety of Storm hammers dated to the time it was wielded by the mythical Chessentan hero Cevalias who was enamored by Saphia, the daughter of a ruler of Cimbar, who manipulated the hero and his Storm hammer into becoming instrumental in elevating Cimbar to the status of the nation's capital.

More common versions of Storm with a simpler +1 enchantment were forged by Master Blacksmith Marrok of the Shining Knight Arms and Armor shop of Neverwinter to help the heroes who sought the cure for the dreaded Wailing Death of the . Later the same year, more powerful versions were created by Master Blacksmith Barun of Beorunna's Well to help the forces of Neverwinter stand against Lady Aribeth the Betrayer, who led a marching army of Luskan in the deadly but short-lived Neverwinter–Luskan war.

## Stalactite Forest

The Stalactite Forest was a landmark located in Skullport.

Description
The Stalactite Forest was suspended above the Central Port. It was a dense concentration of large stalactites that resembled the fangs of a colossal maw. Concealed among these stone formations were vertical passageways utilized by creatures capable of vertical or aerial movement, including drow and beholders.

In response to the scarcity of habitable space, some residents of Skullport constructed dwellings and commercial establishments between, and occasionally within, the stone columns. However, on rare occasions, entire buildings collapsed, resulting in the catastrophic fall of stone and timber onto the areas below.

The Stalactite Forest also served as a hunting ground for various predatory creatures from Undermountain, drawn to the lights and activity of Skullport. Species commonly found in this area included cloakers, lurkers, mobats, and numerous varieties of spiders. The remains of unwary victims were often left suspended from the stalactites, catwalks, or rigging.

## Stane Opera House

The Stane Opera House was a prestigious theater in the city of Ravens Bluff in the 14 century DR, so named for its ownership by the Stane family. While only moderately profitable, it was frequently a haunt of the Ravenian nobility and affluent alike, and thus managed to keep its doors open through the backing and bankrolling of several noble families.

Location
This building stood along much of Lamorgyr's Ride, in the Tentowers neighborhood of the Uptown District. Facing away from the building, the district-spanning street Fireleap Way ran by it.

Structure
The Opera House was a modest, three stories tall structure, made of black marble in emulation of Ravengard House, and had a large dome on its roof. At some point an exterior box office was added to the structure.Appearances of the Opera House prior to No Stone Unturned featured no box office and furthermore its first appearance, The Phantom of Ravens Bluff, had described the foyer as being where one would have to go in order to purchase a ticket. Therefore, it can be surmised that this box office was a later addition.

The black marble used in its construction was sourced from Stonethrust Quarrying, whilst the architecture of the building was designed by Mulsunder.

Interior
The small foyer of the theater acted as both its lobby and a ticket sales space. Arrayed along its eastern wall were several portraits of Opera house actors, with a small ticket desk sat before them. The northern wall of the room held double doors, framed on either side by red velvet curtains, that lead into the auditorium.

Auditorium Area
The main seating area of the theater was its auditorium, which had velvet curtains strewn across it walls. The auditorium seating for about a hundred people, elevated into three levels, all chairs firmly secured to the ground. Seating was divided by two pathways, that lead toward the stage, into three sections. On the left and right side of the auditorium were spiral staircases, leading up to the four balconies booths that stretched across either side of the theater, separated by a waist-high wall.

Each booth held seating for four, what were pairs of plush chairs, two in the front and two in the back. One balcony in particular, designated "1B", had a hidden secret door set in one of its walls. This secret passageway was a long flight of stairs, leading down into the theater's wardrobe area. For a time, due to threats posed by an entity called The Phantom, the booth was roped off and had a sign reading "CLOSED" in the Common tongue hung over its entryway.

The auditorium's roof was host to a pulley system of cables and ropes, most of which lead to a massive chandelier that hung overhead of the audience. The lighting system had its own dedicated room of levers, with one large lever controlling a rather large central rope of the chandelier. Above the lever was a big sign that read "do not touch" in Common.

The original chandelier, worth around 750 gp, held hundreds of candles and had nearly a thousand crystals dangling from its frame, In 1368 DR, it was cut from its bindings by an enigmatic figure called The Phantom and sent plummeting to the ground. A few months later, it had been replaced with a magical chandelier. The theater had a number of other quite large and magnificent chandeliers as well, no two of which matched and were likely sourced from Sembia. They were said to tinkle and chime whenever the Opera House's singers really got into the swing of things. When performances went on, the lights in the auditorium would be dimmed, whilst those centered on the stage would be brightened.

Stage Area
There was a  gap between the audience and the stage. A large restraining wall would later be constructed to further separate the stage from the audience. Situated  below the house floor was its orchestra pit, filled with music stands and chairs for the musicians to sit upon. East of the pit was a gentle rising slope and north of it stood a door directly leading under the stage. This crawlspace was empty, save for a ladder leading up to a trapdoor in the center of the stage. From this side, the trapdoor could be bolted shut.

The stage proper rose  above the theater floor and took up about a third of the Opera house's space. Overhead of the stage was an archway, which served to frame it for the audience. East of the stages were several doors to parts of the backstage and the manager's office, whilst mounted on the west wall were a set of bars and ropes with four corresponding levers. Acting as stop brakes, these levers were part of a large pulley system, allowing stagehands to raise and lower scenery set pieces that were hung up high from metal bars.

Backstage Areas
Backstage were two general, gender segregated dressing rooms, one for men and one for women. Both rooms were moderately sized spaces with dressing tables and racks of costumes. They each had a mirror that dominated their northern wall and a window in their eastern wall that looked out over the side street. The window in the women's dressing room had a comparatively poor view of the street. Additionally, there was a singular, smaller dressing room for the Opera House's starlet. It was furnished with a costume rack, a single chair, and a mirrored dressing table that dominated much of the small space. Following the tragic death of a starlet in 1368 DR, the room was barred from further use.

By far the largest room in the backstage side of the Opera House was its rehearsal room. It was sparsely furnished, save for a few chairs, music stands, and a piano. The eastern wall was covered in mirrors, along which ran a long wooden bar. The room was also host to the theater's back door and a hidden door behind one of the mirror panels, revealing a small, closet-like space.

The next largest room was the storage space for props, with little oddities scattered about haphazardly. Against one wall stood an armory of prop weapons and armor, with a sign above the weapon rack that read "do not touch" in Common. In addition to painted wood prop spears and swords, there were retractable daggers with hidden compartments for packets of theatrical blood, rapiers with soft tips, a real +1 shield, and a paper mache suit of plate armor. Unbeknownst to the manager, this suit of armor was actually a magic item and could impart real protection to a wearer.

Then there was the wardrobe room, the deceptively large workspace of the Opera House's tailors. The room seemed smaller than it actually was on account of the countless racks of costuming, mannequins, and boxes of fabric. There was a mirror mounted to one of its walls. And hidden within one of its corners was trapdoor, whose ladder lead down into the sewers of Ravens Bluff.

And finally, there was a small storage space for cleaning supplies and very odds and ends. With such things as boxes, brooms, mops, and shelves with theater-centric supplies like hairbrushes and makeup.

Other Rooms
The office of the theater manager was lavishly furnished. In addition to a solid oaken desk and matching chair, situated beneath a portrait of one of the theater's early managers, it had a couch and three additional chairs for guests. The desk contained a strongbox of theater earnings, an account ledger, as well as various standard desk supplies like ink, parchment, and quills. Behind the portrait was a hidden storage compartment, a shelf recessed into the wall.

There was also a library in the Opera House, whose shelves were filled to bursting with books that primarily contained plays an operas. By some accounts, most of these theater pieces were mediocre. The room overall was lightly used, as evident by a thin layer of dust that could be found on most things therein.

Services
The Stane Opera House put on a number of abstract musical performances and seasonal operas for the more refined upper pallets of the Ravenian elite. Many of its operatic forms were notably quite experimental. In times when interest in the theater waned, the Opera House was open to being rented out and it allowed a local bardic group called The Burning Truth to perform on its stage.

Inhabitants
The Stane Family Opera House was owned and operated by the Stane family, initially by one Devnar Stane. Following his death, ownership of the theater fell to his brother Archibald Stane. Even after assuming control, Archibald would keep his brother Devnar's portrait hung on the southern wall of his office.

The theater employed a wide number of musicians, actors, and dancers who were all quite adept at their craft. Though some would argue that a few of their performances were less than stellar. Additionally, a number of tailors worked at the theater, fitting people for their costumes, numbering at least four in total.

For a time in the mid-14 century DR, the theater's main starlet and soprano was a woman by the name of Crystal Dawning, who worked under the tutelage of Madame Dillon. After Crystal died in a freak accident, her understudy Mary Cyndcardys would take over from her.

History
Around the, a young newcomer to the stage by the name of Weston LaCroix performed at the Opera house. Things went horribly awry for the actor on that fateful night, being laughed off the stage, and in his anguished flight from the stage stumbled into a host of lanterns that had been carelessly left out. The tormented Weston caught fire and in a panic ran through the theater. He would survive the incident, but with terrible burns on the left side of his face.

Weston devolved into a recluse, living within the city sewers and the secret passages of the Theater, hell bent on making sure no one else would get to act there again. Over time Weston would cause a number of "strange occurrences" within the theater. That were all brushed off as flukes, but that all changed on the day he murdered theater manager Devnar Stane, leaving him to be found in his office decapitated. With that incident it became cemented among the Opera House's staff that the theater was being "haunted" by an entity that they dubbed "The Phantom".

Weston's strange happenings died down following Devnar's death, as did operation of the theater in general, and word of The Phantom would not spread beyond its walls. When the Stane Opera House reopened its doors in the, The Phantom began to strike anew. Weston issued multiple written warnings to the theater, advising against its renewal, eventually resorting to murdering a member of the orchestra. He stabbed the man through his heart with his own violin bow, then strung him up from the ceiling.

This show of force brought Archibald to close the Opera House once more and a massive search for The Phantom was conducted, through it bore no fruit. The new staff gossiped furiously, speculating that The Phantom was some kind of demon or devil that had laid a curse on the Opera House. Concerned for both his own reputation and that of the theater's, Archibald made all members of staff swear a vow of silence on the matter. The Phantom would go on to make demands that balcony seat 1B be permanently closed off and, not wishing for any further bloodshed, Archibald complied.

In the, the theater was underway in its first seasonal opera production, a performance of The Masquerade. However, as the night of the opera inched closer, soprano Crystal Dawning began to take ill. She had caught sight of The Phantom within the rehearsal room one night and tailed him to his hidden lair within the sewers. Enamored by her appearance, he cast some type of charm spell upon her.It is never specified in The Phantom of Ravens Bluff exactly what charm spell the eponymous Phantom cast on Crystal Dawning, nor does his stat-block feature any kind of spell that would do the effects that she is under. Archibald tried to explain away her odd behavior to the chorus as being mere fatigue, but the starlet became increasingly obsessed with that enigmatic figure. Before long gossip clamored through Opera House, saying that her state was The Phantom's work, and that he was sure to whisk Crystal away.

With Crystal now under his sway, The Phantom concocted a plan of robbery, instructing Miss Dawning to steal all of the valuables from Archibald's office and to take them with her when he comes to retrieve her on the night of The Masquerade. Afterwards, the two of them would frighten the rest of the audience, making them flee from the Opera House. Eventually, two days away from opening night, The Phantom left a letter on Archibald's desk that read,

Feeling little other choice, Archibald had a job offer posted up outside the Drooling Dragon Inn, seeking adventurers to provide security for five gold pieces per day. Unbeknownst to him, The Phantom sent Crystal Dawning a bouquet of roses within a vase that day, accompanied by a note that read,

A group of around six adventurers, strapped for cash and in need of work, would end up visiting the Opera House to answer Archibald's job posting. When they came to his office, Archibald explained how tomorrow was to be the opening night for The Masquerade and he wanted Crystal Dawning kept safe. He scoffed at the danger posed by The Phantom, confident that the adventurers could handle him if he showed up.

However, Archibald was rather tight-lipped with them about the Phantom affair, not wanting to risk word getting out to the general Ravenian public and costing him business. It was only with some coaxing that the adventurers managed to get him to reveal yesterday's letter. He implored the heroes to resolve the matter quickly and quietly, though also desired being credited with whatever plan ultimately liberated the Opera House from the terror of The Phantom.

Hired on, the adventurers proceeded to snoop around the Opera house for a bit, questioning people and looking for clues. Just as they were about to investigate the room beneath the stage, they heard the hysterical screams of two chorus girls, crying out "Help! Help! It's the Phantom!" When they rushed to see what was wrong, they found a hanged dummy with a note attached to it that read, "Here swings Archibald." Archibald then arrived, alongside Crawl and Madame Dillon. The manager excused them to his office, but on the way Crystal slipped the adventurers a note that read, "Meet me in balcony 2A in one hour". Back at his office, a sobbing Archibald told them the story of the murdered violinist and confided in them that he was afraid for his own life as well.

Archibald then filled the six adventurers in on his plan. Two of them were to perform in The Masquerade, under the minor roles of servants of Crystal Dawning, acting as her bodyguards. The other four were to wait in the wings as backup, free to do as they pleased so long as it did not disturb the dress performance. When they showed some reluctance, Archibald offered a 5 gp pay raise as well as a gemstone or two.

Over a bell later, fully fit in colorful and dainty costumes for their performance, the adventurers met up with Crystal Dawning. She warned them to look out for themselves, even advising them to leave and forget about what they've learned, for "the Phantom knows and sees all that happens here." During this confrontation, Madame Dillon pulled one of the adventurers aside and confided in them of Crystal's strange behaviors of late and the story of Weston LaCroix. Before further questioning could be had of either, the dress rehearsal was called.

The rehearsal largely went smoothly, with the two costumed adventurers only standing on stage for a period of ten minutes. Just as they were making their way off stage, The Phantom struck a day ahead of schedule. Under the effects of the spells fly and invisibility, 10' radius, he landed atop the chandelier and cut its ropes, creating hysteria and panic among the theater staff. Amidst this opportune confusion, Crystal Dawning fled to Archibald's office to enact their robbery. As the chandelier was halfway to the ground, The Phantom hopped off it and flew towards Crystal, ready to cast color spray on any adventurers there waiting to stop them. The two then made their escape together down the stage's trapdoor.

Unwilling to let The Phantom get away with his heist, the six adventurers chased after them down through the city sewers, coming across two dead ends, several monsters, and the corpse of the violinist. All the while, taunted from afar by the mad bard. Eventually they found themselves at The Phantom's haven. Behind an oaken door they could hear the man's voice, yelling at Crystal to leave and then begging her cease something before letting out a blood curdling scream.

Entering, they took in the gruesome sight of a sobbing Crystal Dawning, clutching a bloody dagger with a limp hand. She was poised over the body of a dark cloaked figure, pooling in blood. They would soon discover this to all be an elaborate ruse of props taken from the theater – theater blood, a mere prop dagger, and the body no more than a mannequin. Meanwhile, the true Phantom was flying overhead, keeping quiet until he was ready to make a grand entrance.

Crystal shouted at the adventurers to stay back, threatening to end her own life if they came closer. She theatrically cried, "I had to
kill him...he was too ill-fated for this cruel, cruel world. Go away, and allow me to suffer my grief alone!" The moment the adventurers let their guard down, Crystal leapt back and The Phantom sprung to action, shouting "Ever surprised, are fools!" and firing off a magic missile. He fought the adventurers to the very death, all the while Crystal interfering on occasion on The Phantom's behalf. As he laid dying, Weston LaCroix refused to reveal where he hid Archibald's valuables and delusionally proclaimed that he would rise from the dead one day to exact his revenge.

With Weston's death, Crystal Dawning was at last freed from the clutches of his charm spell. She told the adventurers everything she knew, emphasizing how she was coerced, and then revealed a shocking letter. Addressed to The Phantom, it said the author was going to commit to delivering Crystal to the specter. Whether the adventurers realized it or not, the handwriting was that of Archibald's, the man more than willing to give up the soprano in order to save his own theater.The Phantom of Ravens Bluff presents the possibility of the players presenting Archibald's note to the authorities and getting him arrested on charges of conspiracy, after which ownership of the theater would fall to Madame Dillon and it would come to be renamed the Dillon Opera House. This series of events can be presumed to have not taken place, as Archibald is still running the theater when next seen in Monday's Child.

Several months later, in the month of Eleasias, Crystal Dawning was found dead in the bath. Her death was ruled to be an accident, caused by acid that had fallen from a shelf above and into her bathing waters, but the next day a note was found over the tub. The next day, a group of adventurers working for the City Watch's Investigative Unit to track down a serial killer, would visit the Stane Opera House to do some questioning and look around for clues. Searching the shelves above Crystal's bathtub, they discovered a leather scrollcase containing a note that read, "Tuesday's child is full of grace."Though the adventure Monday's Child uses the Germanic tradition of names for the days of the week, the Faerûnian week has no proper names for its days. Furthermore, the adventure makes the incorrect assumption that the Calendar of Harptos divided its months into seven-day blocks, whereas it actually divides them into three blocks of ten days each.

Sometime later in the 14 century DR, the alchemist Silac Decor scaled the Opera House and from its rooftop tried to use an object called the orb of storms to destroy the DeVillars Estate.

In the, whilst posing as Jaer Kell Wildhame, a minor noble from the Vilhon Reach, the rogue Jack Ravenwild received an invitation from Lord and Lady Flermeer to join them at their box in the Stane Opera House for a performance of The Bride of Secomber. He would end up attending later that evening, after having designed a mock coat of arms for the Wildhames.

## Storoper

The storoper, a portmanteau of stone and roper, also called tar roper, was a creature very similar to the roper, in that they would rope in their prey with  tentacles.

Description
Standing  high and  wide, they looked like small statues of ordinary ropers. Weighing some, with gaping maws and six tentacles, they could sense movement up to some  away. The stony exterior of the storopers made them immune to ordinary missile fire from arrows and bolts.

Combat
Once the storoper sensed prey, it would become completely still, awaiting its target's approach. When only  away from its prey, three of the six tentacles would fling out to hit the prey. From the tentacles a venom would inject into the target, which would first immobilize, then confuse and dominate the affected individual. For the next minute or so, the affected prey would fight for the storoper against anyone else near it. Ideally the storoper would use all six tentacles to hit two individuals at once, so as to maximize its chances of overwhelming the nearby prey group. After the storoper had launched its vicious venom attack, it would attempt to drag prey into its maw much as normal ropers did.

Ecology
The storopers could, once dead, be pried open by hammer and chisel to access whatever non-organic valuables they had consumed recently.

History
Storopers were known to hunt in the deeper parts of Southkrypt, deep underground around .

Likewise in the deepest parts of fallen Tethyamar, where the mines and Underdark connected, storopers were to be found, feeding on the other creatures there hunting for ores and gems.

## Stele

A stele  were slabs erected in many parts of the Realms as monuments. Often made of stone, their surfaces were covered in inscriptions, sometimes of an ornamental nature, ornamental carvings, or both. The reasons for their creation could vary significantly, from marking territorial boundaries, to funerary purposes, or to document or commemorating historical events or personages.

Notable Menhirs
 In Avernus, the Crypt of the Hellriders held four memorial steles, inscribed necromantically with the names of all the Hellriders who fell whilst fighting at Zariel's side. These steles binded the spirits of those Hellriders, tethering them to the crypt and thus forcing them to linger on as ghosts. However, the steles were protected by necrotic energy so long as the soul-bound parchments in the crypt were unharmed.
 In the ancient city-state of Cursrah, stelae were used for funerary purposes.
 In the Chultan Peninsula, the ancient yuan-ti city of Ssy'in'tia'saminass had stone inscribed with Draconic runes.
 Gravenhollow, a mystical library in the Underdark, kept some of its ancient records inscribed upon the surfaces of stelae.
 In north Faerûn, the over a dozen ogre tribes of Thar used stone stelae to mark their territory. They were pieces of notable artistry, carved with all manner of subject matter, from the ogre god Vaprak vanquishing his enemies, to ancient heroes and monsters, to seemingly human priests summoning ibrandlin to terrorize the ogres. The art style of carvings was noted by some as being reminescent of carvings found further west, among the Ffolk and the Northmen of the Moonshae Isles. These stelae were also frequently inscribed with an ornamental runic script, potentially the remnants of ancient written language among the ogres of Thar, and each tribe had its own signature rune. Whilst art collectors would likely pay a great deal for them, the ogres were highly protective of their stelae, even going so far as to pursue thieves beyond Thar. Additionally, many of them were imbued with curses by tribal shamans.
 In the Plane of Fire, the City of Brass had a road famous for the stelae that lined it, known as the Street of Stelae. The stelae that lined it were inscribed with the victories of the efreeti over the other races of the plane of fire, as well as the spoils they claimed.
 Deep in the jungles of Far Payit, around 80 stelae known as "tree-stones" were erected all throughout the Ixtzul Valley. Outside of the city of Ixtzul, these columns of white granite stood  and were carved with ornate, ornamental glyphs. At the tops of the colemns resided a stylized head of H'Calos the Star Worm, a strange creature from beyond the stars who was trapped beneath the city of Ixtzul with a great binding spell. These stelae were tied to the preservation of this binding spell and as such radiated a strong magical aura. Within the city of Ixtzul itself, there were even more stelae scattered throughout its Great Plaza, that acted as the primary binding points for the creature. Though similarly topped with a stylized representation of H'Calos, these stelae were only  in height and each inscribed with the exploits  of one Revered Counselor.
 In the Haunted Lands of Zakhara, the people of Sokkar used steles for funerary purposes. Regardless of the deceased's station in life, tombs in Sokkar always featured both steles and a ka figure. They were typically decorated in intricate carvings depicting scenes of the deceased dining, hunting, praying, sleeping, praying, or playing what were their favorite games and sporting activities in life. Whilst the ka figures were believed to hold a deceased's ka (soul), lining the walls of a tomb with these stone slabs were said to ensure that the deceased could perform the depicted enjoyable activities throughout their time in the afterlife.
 In the Outlands, the gate-town of Rigus had large granite steles erected as memorials, engraved with the names of fallen heroes.

History
When Edimu, a beloved horse from Jazirat al-Sayyad, passed from the world a mausoleum was constructed for him in Sokkar. Placed within this mausoleum was a stele, depicting Edimu galavanting in the hills of a fertile island, along with an inscription in Chun that labeled it "Jazirat al-Sayyad." It was accompanied by a life-sized ka figure made of alabaster, adorned with a golden bit and bridle. The bridle was encrusted in diamonds and sapphires, as well as inscribed with Chun runes that bore Edimu's name and wishes for a long, happy afterlife. However, ghouls later looted the chambers and stole the horse's bit and bridle, breaking both his ka figure and stele in the process, and thus untethering his spirit from the afterlife.

## Stormbanner Wolves

The Stormbanner Wolves were the fearsome Northlander defenders and raiders of Rogarsheim on Norland.

Activities
These forces were concerned with defending their realm from the threat of giants from the south of Norland, which they did alongside the other inhabitants of the island including the Ffolk. They also focused much of their energies on attacking Amn's colonies in the Moonshaes, especially by sinking the Amnian merchant vessels that traveled the Sea of Swords between the Sword Coast and Snowdown.

History
As of the mid–14 century DR, the forces of Rogarsheim comprised a fleet of six longships (the largest on Norland), each crewed by forty battle-ready sailors. This fleet boasted two ships crewed by elite fighters (twice as many as the other kingdoms of Norland), and one of these crews had been handpicked by the king to be the most skilled combatants on the whole of Norland.In FR2 Moonshae (1987), Rogarsheim is mistakenly referred to in the text as "Rottesheim".

As of the late 15 century DR, despite a century of peace with the Ffolk under the United Moonshae Isles, the Stormbanner Wolves retained a warlike tradition that kept them culturally distinct and continually suspicious of their neighbors around the Moonshae Isles, especially Alaron.

The river originated in the peaks of the Storm Horns northwest of Tyrluk, flowing south from glacial melts high up in the clouds near Tumblerock Pass, Rungnir's glacier, and the lair of the white dragon Nexxylplyx.
